issues.item: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Life not worth living anymore' suggests a marked hopeless/depressive or self-destructive appraisal. The rest of the selected items center on fragmented trauma memory and avoidance/social distraction, without other items indicating pervasive defeat, guilt, permanent damage, or a threat-related meaning that would make this severe appraisal cohere strongly.

vignette: When the van's tires surrendered to the highway's black ice, Mateo's world became a spinning cage of twisting metal and shattering glass. He woke to the hiss of his own breath and the relentless drumming of rain through a cracked window, pinned beneath a collapsed support beam. For hours, trapped in that silent, freezing dark, he waited for a rescue that felt impossibly distant. When he finally crawled free, the physical cuts and bruises healed, but the narrative of the accident fractured immediately. He found it difficult to deliberately remember what happened; his mind offered only disconnected flashes-a blinding headlight, the acrid smell of burning rubber, the sudden sensation of weightlessness. He felt like he was only remembering parts of what happened, with the rest of the timeline missing entirely, leaving him with an incomplete picture he could never piece together. The event was potent because the terror of that entrapment never left his nervous system; any confined space or sudden loud noise immediately pulled him back to the roof pressing down on him, making the past feel as immediate as the present. As the weeks passed, Mateo's interpretation of the crash hardened into rigid beliefs. He became fixated on the injustice of the situation, certain that nothing had been done about the road conditions that caused the skid, and that the insurance company had abandoned him. This conviction of profound unfairness, coupled with a gnawing dread that he would not be able to control his anger and would do something terrible if forced to face the event, began to dictate his daily life. Because he was certain that life had been destroyed and terrified of his own potential rage, he actively suppressed any attempt to deliberately recall the accident. His negative appraisals directly shaped his memory strategy, leading him to consciously block out the event rather than face the gaps. The more he convinced himself that his future was ruined, the less he allowed himself to examine the trauma, ensuring his recall remained stubbornly suppressed. The unresolved gaps in his memory did not remain quiet. Each fragmented piece that breached his defenses felt unmoored and dangerous, threatening to unravel his composure. The memory fragmentation directly deepened his negative appraisals, reinforcing his conviction that life was destroyed and justice would never come. In direct response, Mateo began constantly socialising, keeping himself constantly surrounded by people so he was never alone with his thoughts. He would linger at the club where he performed, forcing conversations about setlists and gear while strictly avoiding talking about the event or its aftermath. The fragmented nature of his recall directly fueled this maladaptive strategy, pushing him toward crowded rooms to outrun the silent moments. Conversely, the constant socialising and deliberate avoidance of thinking about the crash actively prevented his brain from processing the trauma, which in turn kept his memories stubbornly fragmented. Every quiet moment in his soundproofed home studio or empty car became a threat he could no longer manage, so he filled the space with noise and company, ensuring the gaps in his recollection never settled. Over months, this loop tightened. His fear of losing control and his sense of ruined life grew heavier with each unexamined memory fragment, making him more desperate for constant socialising. Meanwhile, the very crowd of people he sought out only highlighted his isolation, reinforcing his belief that life was destroyed and justice would never come. Now, three years later, Mateo sits across from a clinician, his hands drumming a restless rhythm on his knees. A recent missed gig and the realization that he can no longer drive to late-night rehearsals without panic brought him here. He hopes someone can help him stop running, though he remains terrified that remembering will finally make him snap, or that he will never play music again.
